searchText: Could someone explain this test to me: ``` ./eofdump eof --hex 0xef0001010004020001000e04000000008000045f6000e100025f5f6000e1fffd00 0 PUSH0 0 &{0 0} [0] 1 PUSH1 1 &{1 1} [2] 3 RJUMPI 2 &{2 2} [5 7] 6 PUSH0 2 &{1 1} [6] 7 PUSH0 2 &{2 2} [7] 8 PUSH1 3 &{1 3} [9] 10 RJUMPI 4 &{2 4} [12 9] 13 STOP 4 &{1 3} [13] ok. ``` It should error with `EOF_ConflictingStackHeight`, is it because the RJUMPI self-references? Which rule guards against that? This is about having same stack height for backward jumps Weird, I do have a rule for that Where is your code? ```go // target reached via backwards jump nextBounds, ok := stackBounds[nextPC] if !ok { return 0, ErrInvalidBackwardJump } change := int(params.StackLimit) - jt[nextOP].maxStack + jt[nextOP].minStack if have, want := nextBounds.max+change, currentBounds.max; have != want { return 0, fmt.Errorf("%w want %d as max got %d at pos %d,", ErrInvalidBackwardJump, want, have, pos) } if have, want := nextBounds.min+change, currentBounds.min; have != want { return 0, fmt.Errorf("%w want %d as min got %d at pos %d,", ErrInvalidBackwardJump, want, have, pos) } ``` I am getting `BackwardJumpBiggestNumMismatch` so it is about `max_stack_height` This update to EOF testing is going to land soon: https://github.com/ethereum/execution-spec-tests/pull/613 Not nuclear change fortunately (based on the number of modified tests). Yep, I still don't get it. Its one of the last tests that I can't pass My old version got a stack underflow there I'll try to debug this manually. Can you explain this notation? ``` 3 RJUMPI 2 &{2 2} [5 7] ``` position, opcode, maxStackHeight, stackbounds (min, max) and the following instructions (-1) in the next line The second RJUMPI calls itself And pops one item from the stack, so it should result in an underflow at some point? Ah I figured it out I think ``` if currentStackMax != nextBounds.max { return 0, ErrInvalidBackwardJump } ``` This clause was missing I think `RJUMPI` calling itself is always a failure 🙂 yes, because it will run down the stack to 0 I'm passing all tests of ethereum/tests except for two now, but those two were also not passed by my previous implementation For `RJUMP` itself the algo compares stack after with stack before and they are never equal as `RJUMP` pops one item nice. you should try https://github.com/ethereum/execution-spec-tests/releases/tag/eip7692%40v1.0.1 now 🙂 was in the call, here is code that throws this: https://github.com/bluealloy/revm/blob/561fbdbb117a5613475a8f099981a36fedd0104b/crates/interpreter/src/interpreter/analysis.rs#L522 > Passed 984 tests out of 986 the EEST may be already superior to ethereum/tests tell me what's failing ``` Executing Tests: jumpf_backward.json 0, Prague: expected success, got unreachable code Executing Tests: rjumpi_max_backward.json 0, Prague: expected success, got invalid backward jump ``` In the first `JUMPF` works as terminating instruction (?) Anyway, in the test itself there should be an ID allowing for finding the test source: https://github.com/ethereum/execution-spec-tests/blob/main/tests/prague/eip7692_eof_v1/eip4200_relative_jumps/test_rjumpi.py#L256 Yes, the problem is that my implementation requires the following rule: - A section that is not visited by a previous section is unreachable Since we have 0 -> 2 -> 1, we don't know when validating 1 that it can be reached by 2. I have to rewrite my algorithm for scheduling the visits Sounds like dp to me dp? I thinking if we can/should require this to be in order Dynamic Programming I fixed it now https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/29518/commits/a89872c5f045b8e01266f346c9444662b4146787 This is the diff, I think we will loose something if we require the sections to be in order though Yeah, I think we also have a queue here. Is this still the main EOF channel? Is there any appetite for including an ORIGIN ban in the first version of EOF? Yes Easy to do technically, but I think this would need to go though All-Core-Devs meeting. The ol' runaround. 😂 On the ACD call, they said it would need to be decided here first. And as part of that I had asked for some commentary from security auditors supporting this change. The ball is in your court to provide this. More than a lukewarm "This would be neat" but more of an endorsement of "this will improve the security of EOF" So, no, not runaround. Awaiting further information. Hang on, the conclusion from EOF call was that it's technically feasible but not up to eof to decide. It's up to ACD. And in ACD is also where I made my second opinion request. I don't care if it comes in ACD or the EOF calls, I'm pushing back without it. With all due respect, I'm not going to do this. It is *well* established by now that ORIGIN sucks and serves no real purpose. Banning its continued misuse in EOF would be an easy win that everyone *should* agree on. Not sure what spinning up any auditors would accomplish. If that is the case you can get at least one other person with credeitials to back that statement up. I've had private conversations with some people who feel the opposite, so I will need some public evidence other than a claim it's "well established by now" Can they point to a legitimate use case? I feel like alias ORIGIN to SENDER and ban ORIGIN in EOF have gotten confused in the air here. aliasing ORIGIN to SENDER went over like a lead balloon this is about banning ORIGIN in EOF Gonna need more than a use case and an argument. What would persuade me is a second concurring opinion. Hard to parse the back and forth of this chat, but v was initially supportive of either the alias or the ban. Not sure if he still is. https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/718596092828057631/1210829500632539156 https://github.com/ethereum/solidity/issues/683 This thread is a discussion of all the reasons ORIGIN sucks. The consensus of the thread was to not remove it from *Solidity*, though which is a completely different subject than banning it in EOF. But the consensus *was* that ORIGIN sucks. To disclaim: banning ORIGIN in EOF does nothing for me. After all, it's a future-facing fix. I just like to get rid of bad tech debt whenever possible. What was the basis for their hesitation on an ORIGIN ban in EOF? (Or were they still thinking about the aliasing?) What consensus? It seems you just posted two threads where people enthusiastically _defend_ the usefulness of tx.origin Any perceived use case mentioned can and should be done some other way. It was a private conversation. Based on that, however, what matters to me is a second opinion stating that banning ORIGIN in EOF is a good idea and would be effective. Well it's self-evident that banning ORIGIN in EOF would be effective at stopping people from using ORIGIN. They could still work around it with legacy deployments, of course. I've made my position clear, and I don't think it's an unreasonable ask. I am going to disengage until a second party actively supports this position. Anybody know how to get in touch with Peter Borah? 😂
